articles.title_orig: A fire devastates the Eagle’s Nest retreat built for Hitler in Germany. A suspect is detained
articles.title_zh: A fire devastates the Eagle’s Nest retreat built for Hitler in Germany. A suspect is detained
articles.content_orig:
About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern Germany
German police have arrested a suspect after a fire ripped through Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat in Bavaria, leaving the historic Nazi meeting place – known as the Eagle’s Nest – largely destroyed.
About 200 firefighters were deployed on Friday night to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote, purpose-built Kehlsteinhaus residence, a protected building on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany .
Flames rose high into the air as firefighters approached the scene to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said.
“A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the fire.
Lisa Maier, a police spokesperson, said firefighters struggled to tackle the blaze due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft).
The building, which was one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era, was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.
Built by the Nazis and formally inaugurated by Hitler on his birthday in 1939, the Eagle’s Nest has been preserved as a monument to “the insanity of the regime”, according to its website .
It is only accessible via a road cut into the mountain through previously impassable terrain. Nazis would enter a tunnel and take a 124-metre brass lift buried in the mountain to get inside the building.
Authorities were alerted to the fire when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.15pm, police said. When firefighters arrived on the scene at about 9.50pm, the entire building was engulfed in flames.
No reason for the fire was given, but German media reported that investigators suspected it was the result of arson. Firefighters found no one inside the building, which was reportedly still burning at 7am on Saturday.
Fire departments from six municipalities sent emergency personnel to tackle the blaze and the Bavarian Red Cross, the local mountain rescue service and the police also attended.
The blaze appeared to be out later on Saturday morning, although smoke continued to rise from the building.
A police spokesperson told the German tabloid Bild: “It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved.” Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an Agence France-Presse photographer.
Maier said police were still investigating and would hold a news conference later on Saturday.
According to Bild, a motorcyclist whom local police officers came across on their way to the scene had been arrested, but his involvement in the fire remains unclear and a police spokesperson declined to release information about his identity.
The Eagle’s Nest was constructed between 1937 and 1938 and forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and communists in the Holocaust.
It became legendary in the postwar period and was often depicted as an essential meeting place in US war films, although in reality Hitler rarely visited the complex.
Since 1952 the building has housed an exhibition by the Institute for Contemporary History recounting its Nazi history, and a restaurant.
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Kim Jong-un Makes First Visit to China in Over a Year
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong-un Makes First Visit to China in Over a Year
articles.content_orig:
North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member
Kim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour.
The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency.
He met Wang Huning, a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party. The pair toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship.
Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries”, according to Xinhua.
Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, Xinhua said.
The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of Kim’s ties with Beijing ahead of the 25 October anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean war, which came days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950.
Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum about China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.
Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.
The 3km bridge opened in mid-October , 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border, leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.
The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June , his first trip there in seven years.
Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.
Xi will host the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.
Reuters reported on Friday , however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.
Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Engadget Review Recap: iPhone Duo, Rivian R2 And More
articles.title_zh: Engadget Review Recap: iPhone Duo, Rivian R2 And More
articles.content_orig:
A roundup of recent reviews from Engadget.
We've reached the point of the tech calendar where the pace of new devices is just absurd. Over the last two weeks, the team here at Engadget has published over a dozen reviews. That in-depth testing runs the gamut from Switch 2 controllers to repairable laptops and a new Alexa tablet to unique wireless microphones . I can't fit all of them in this roundup, so be sure to check out our reviews hub after you read up on the biggest recently tested products below.
There's no doubt the iPhone Duo was one of the most-anticipated devices of the year. Surprisingly, Apple's first attempt at a folding phone doesn't seem like a first-generation device. Yes, it's heavy and expensive, and many apps still need to be optimized for its interior screen, but there's a lot to like here if you can afford one.
"The company had the luxury to learn from its competitors' accomplishments and missteps, which means the iPhone Duo has sidestepped most of the growing pains a new class of gadget might normally encounter," senior reviews reporter Sam Rutherford said.
Before he set off folding the latest iPhone, Sam spent some time behind the wheel of the mid-sized Rivian R2 . He discovered a roomy SUV with great power and range, and an interior that checks all the boxes. There's fine-tuning to still be done, and you might want to wait for the base model to arrive next year.
"Rivian is proving that just because an electric SUV is smaller and more affordable, that doesn't mean it has to make major trade-offs to its style, power and tech compared to the rest of its siblings," he said. "For a family of four, the R2 feels like the Goldilocks SUV that could make people who currently drive gas-powered rivals jump to an EV and never look back.:
If you've ever wanted the benefits of a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses without the creepy cameras, there's now a stylish, audio-only option in the Ray-Ban Meta Audio . The frame styles look more like "normal" glasses, they offer longer battery life due to the lack of cameras and, most importantly, they're comfortable to wear.
"One of my favorite things about the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses is just how 'normal' they look and feel," senior reporter Karissa Bell said. "I was still able to enjoy the open-ear speakers and other audio features without being constantly aware that I was wearing smart glasses, or that others around me might notice them."
Technics impressed us in 2025 with its AZ100 true wireless earbuds and now the company has put its magnetic fluid driver tech in a set of over-ear headphones. With the A1000 , the company offers excellent sound quality and ANC performance alongside a comfy design and solid battery life. The two problems? They cost $450 and one of the standout features is unreliable.
"The true wireless AZ100 made a big impression, thanks in part to those Magnetic Fluid drivers, and the A1000 builds on that success with equally impressive sound," contributing reviews writer James Trew said. "Truly, they're a joy to wear and to listen to."
Senior reviews reporter Devindra Hardawar spent the last week testing the first laptop he could get his hands on with NVIDIA's new RTX Spark chip inside: the ASUS ProArt P16 . He discovered an expensive yet extremely powerful laptop that really isn't meant to be used by most of us.
"The ASUS ProArt P16 is an impressive premium laptop, undoubtedly. But its high starting cost and unique hardware make it something that's truly only tempting for AI professionals," he said. "I'd give the entire RTX Spark platform at least a year before I could recommend it to general users or even gamers."

articles.title_orig: Six Flags to Add Seat Belts to Rides Following Death
articles.title_zh: Six Flags to Add Seat Belts to Rides Following Death
articles.content_orig: Six Flags announced Friday night that Goliath and eight other rides remain closed after the deadly Goliath accident and that they’ve begun major safety changes at Six Flags Over Georgia and other parks. [DOWNLOAD: Free WSB-TV News app for alerts as news breaks ] The company said it will be adding seat belts to the Goliath roller coaster “and other coasters with a similar restraint.” “Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia remains closed pending necessary safety reviews and clearances. Eight additional rides at five other parks are temporarily closed out of an abundance of caution,” the park said on its website in a statement attributed to John Reilly, president and CEO, Six Flags Entertainment Corporation. In addition, the company said its conducting a safety review across all its parks. “We have engaged independent engineers and ride inspection specialists to comprehensively review current safety procedures across our entire portfolio of rides and attractions, across all of our parks,” the company said. Hassan Kariem died after falling from the ride earlier this month. Four other riders were hurt. Here is the full press release from Six Flags Over Georgia: To Our Guests and Passholders, Our hearts remain with the family and loved ones of Hassan Kariem, those injured, and everyone impacted by the tragic incident at Six Flags Over Georgia. What happened has deeply affected all of us at Six Flags. Safety has always been fundamental to the experience we provide for our guests. Across our parks, guests have taken more than one billion rides over the past four years, supported by comprehensive safety, maintenance and inspection programs. That commitment requires constant vigilance and determination to continually improve. As we continue to support ongoing investigations, we are building on our commitment to safety in all we do including a focus on these priorities: We will continue to share updates on our progress. An Update on Our Parks Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia remains closed pending necessary safety reviews and clearances. Eight additional rides at five other parks are temporarily closed out of an abundance of caution. Our parks remain open, including throughout Halloween weekend, with more than 220 roller coasters operating across our parks. I know trust is earned through actions and not words. As CEO of Six Flags, I take that responsibility personally. We will continue to communicate about our progress and hold ourselves accountable to our commitments to you. articles.title_orig: Is Washington misreading Beijing? Decline in US visits to China sparks concern
articles.title_zh: Is Washington misreading Beijing? Decline in US visits to China sparks concern
articles.content_orig:
Dwindling academic programmes and official visits risk eroding the next generation of American China specialists
When Grant Newsham, a retired US Marine colonel and security analyst, sat down for an interview that aired last month, he called China’s economic rise illusory and said there were “600 million Chinese at least who live on US$5 a day or less”.
Some commenters argued that uneven development was common across countries. Others questioned how much on-the-ground China experience Newsham had before making the statement to the Epoch Times, a right-wing outlet associated with Falun Gong and banned in China.
However, the debate went beyond a dispute over China’s living standards: it highlighted a need for Americans – including policymakers and academics – to gain first-hand experience of China, while drawing attention to their shrinking opportunities to gain that exposure.

articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Champi nears China after battering Taiwan, Japan
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Champi nears China after battering Taiwan, Japan
articles.content_orig:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

articles.title_orig: China study suggests animal sacrifice may have been part of ancient Sanxingdui rituals
articles.title_zh: China study suggests animal sacrifice may have been part of ancient Sanxingdui rituals
articles.content_orig:
New research, facilitated by cutting-edge techniques, led to one of the first examples of physical proof for ancient ritual animal slaughter
Animal sacrifice has played a major role in human history, from mythological stories about Odysseus to modern rituals such as Nepal’s Gadhimai Festival.
The tradition also dates back to ancient peoples we know little about. A research paper published in the Journal of Archaeological Science in late August suggests that the enigmatic Sanxingdui people likely practised animal sacrifice.
To reach this conclusion, researchers identified what appeared to be a sacrificial pit based on the spatial arrangement of valuable artefacts.

articles.title_orig: Is your Medicare Advantage plan ending next year? Here's what to know
articles.title_zh: Is your Medicare Advantage plan ending next year? Here's what to know
articles.content_orig:
Medicare chief Dr. Mehmet Oz speaks at an event announcing the artificial intelligence website, America.gov  in Washington, D.C., last month. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
A slew of Medicare Advantage plans are disappearing for next year, leaving seniors in many areas with fewer options. In 193 counties across the country, no plans are offered at all.
Medicare's annual open enrollment period kicked off October 15 and runs until December 7, and seniors enrolled in those privatized Medicare plans that are closing in certain markets should carefully review their options.
Medicare Advantage means private insurers run Medicare for older Americans who choose it over traditional Medicare, where the federal government itself administers the program. More than half of the 70 million Americans in Medicare choose Medicare Advantage. It's popular because it covers services like vision and dental, often with lower premiums than traditional Medicare. It also often folds in the "Part D" drug benefit, simplifying that decision.
But a downside of Medicare Advantage is that companies can pick and choose where they offer plans. If a certain community is not profitable, a company can leave that market. And that has been happening on an increasingly large scale the last three years, according to research published in JAMA.
Big swaths of rural America are losing Medicare Advantage choices and so are some major metro areas.
Last year, 2.9 million seniors were in Medicare Advantage plans that closed up shop, according to JAMA. This year, an analysis of insurance company announcements by An Arm and A Leg podcast, shows at least 2 million people will be affected. Other preliminary estimates range from 3.2 million to 5 million seniors. About 35 million people are enrolled in Medicare Advantage.
According to an analysis of federal data by the health policy research organization KFF, the 193 counties that will have zero Medicare Advantage plans are mostly rural. Last year that number was about 120 counties without a plan offered.
KFF's numbers also show that there will be far fewer plans offered in some metro areas. Dallas, Minneapolis, Seattle, Houston and Portland all have between a quarter and a third fewer Medicare Advantage plans for seniors.
If your plan is ending, and you don't choose another, the insurance company will assign you to another Medicare Advantage plan or the government will enroll you in traditional Medicare — but without a supplemental or drug plan.
If you want to switch from Medicare Advantage to traditional Medicare and your plan is ending, you can enroll in a Medicare supplemental plan — also known as Medigap — without the same restrictions that you would normally have. If you have a pre-existing condition that has prevented you from enrolling in Medigap before, that could be good news.
Another wrinkle this year is that insurance companies can cap enrollments on some of the Medicare Advantage plans that they do offer.
Which means: If you wait to sign up, a plan you want might already be full.
The companies are supposed to enroll people on a first-come, first-serve basis — and not cherry-pick customers based on health conditions, age, or demographics.
Another reason not to delay is that with so many people on the hunt for new plans, it may take longer than usual to get help.

articles.title_orig: British woman dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea in the Bahamas
articles.title_zh: British woman dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea in the Bahamas
articles.content_orig:
A woman has died after attempting to rescue her two sons when they were swept away while snorkelling in the Bahamas.
The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of a 36-year-old British woman on Tuesday.
The force said it believed the woman - believed to be from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire - was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
In an attempt to rescue her sons, "the woman was also swept away", police said. The children were subsequently rescued from the water.
In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.
"Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
"Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
"In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
"She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered.
"Foul play is not suspected at this time.
"An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death."
A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

articles.title_orig: Kim Jong Un makes chilling announcement after sister threatened to 'mercilessly eliminate'
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong Un makes chilling announcement after sister threatened to 'mercilessly eliminate'
articles.content_orig:
The North Korean leader revealed his plans to launch a 'military revolution'
North Korea is on a mission to build the 'world's strongest armed forces', according to its leader Kim Jong Un.
The dictator, 42, delivered a determined speech about his future plans for the military and his intention to diversify its defence capabilities earlier this week.
It comes just days after his younger sister Kim Yo Jong issued a warning to South Korea - and all of this suggests their neighbours ought to be on high alert.
While addressing a conference of company commanders for ​North Korea's Army in Pyongyang, Kim issued a rallying cry to those present as he explained a 'new-era military build-up' is on the horizon.
He revealed that he wants North Korea's military branches to transform themselves into self-sufficient combat units, who are capable of carrying out operations independently.
Addressing the sea of army chiefs, Kim outlined how he intends to 'build a strong army in the new era and the duties of company commanders', according to the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
He announced that 'developing the world 's strongest armed forces' was at the top of his nation's agenda and believes this can be achieved by 'fostering the strongest companies and accelerating a military revolution of our own style'.
Kim has always been keen on making North Korea a formidable force, but given the current state of the world and the recent rumours that circulated about his health , his latest comments are being perceived as a show of strength.
Earlier this month, the US -based Chinese dissident Xie Wanjun claimed that Kim had collapsed and fallen into a coma, before being rushed to Beijing for emergency treatment.
Boldly, he then claimed that the North Korean leader had passed away and that his alleged death was being concealed by the regime.
In what appeared to be an attempt to rubbish these allegations, photographs and footage reportedly showing Kim visiting a clothing and footwear exhibition in Pyongyang on 19 October, accompanied by his wife and daughter.
The snaps of him browsing items were deemed to be 'proof of life' following the rumours that run rampant online.
In wake of all this, Kim's sister then flexed the military muscles of North Korea while issuing a warning to the South.
North Korea has been adding mines, barbed wire fences, anti-tank barriers and other fortifications the border - and Kim Yo Jung announced 'psychological warfare' was incoming.
"Our tactical hunting teams are taking new positions, and within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border," she said.
Both sides of Korea have frequently deployed loudspeakers to blast out sounds of their choosing, according to The Guardian , but these speakers have been silent for the last 16 months.
The South usually opts to play K-pop and news critical of Kim Jong Un's nation, while the North reportedly tends to use 'haunting bestial howls'.
Kim Yo Jung warned that border guards in North Korea will 'show no mercy' if there is any 'actual harm to our territorial security and our service persons’ safety'.
Interestingly, South Korean media then reported on Saturday (24 October) that Kim Jong Un has visited China - the place he was said to have perished in - in his first visit to the country for a year.
He is reported to have visited the city of Dandong after crossing a newly opened bridge between the countries.
Topics: Army , World News , Politics , Kim Jong-un
Olivia is a journalist at LADbible Group with more than five years of experience and has worked for a number of top publishers, including News UK. She also enjoys writing food reviews (as well as the eating part). She is a stereotypical reality TV addict, but still finds time for a serious documentary.

articles.title_orig: Still sending checks in the mail? It's time to stop
articles.title_zh: Still sending checks in the mail? It's time to stop
articles.content_orig:
Every application that stalls at an identity check costs a bank or credit union a customer it paid to attract. Yet most institutions judge instant verification by the fraud it stops, counting only the bad applicants it catches and ignoring the good ones it wrongly turns away.
Those numbers leave out a big part of what verification is worth. Speed at that step also decides how many applicants go on to fund their accounts. Standard fraud measures, borrowed from cybersecurity, only look at people who got through verification, so they miss everyone who quit along the way. Counting the drop-offs at each step and the accounts that get funded turns the same data into a record of whether verification is winning customers — or driving them away.
That shift gives fraud controls a bigger role. “If you can get to this place where we don’t catch our good customers at fraud traps, your fraud controls can actually become a growth lever,” says Jeff Scott, general manager of fraud intelligence at Q2, which provides digital banking and fraud prevention software to banks and credit unions. Getting there starts with rethinking when verification happens and what gets measured once it’s done.
Key insight: The data fraud teams already collect can measure growth once it includes the applicants who quit and the accounts that get funded.
The front door is the first stretch of the application, the identity and document checks an applicant hits before an account opens. It’s where both pressures meet: fraudsters attack there, and good applicants decide whether to keep going.
Certainly, attacks are getting harder to stop. The checks institutions relied on for years, a document scan, a credit pull, out-of-wallet questions, are easier to beat with breached data and cheap tools. Entrust, an identity verification provider, analyzed more than 1 billion verifications it ran between September 2024 and September 2025. Digital forgeries made up 35% of document fraud attempts, and deepfakes accounted for a fifth of biometric fraud attempts. Injection attacks, which feed fake images or video straight into a verification system, rose 40% year over year. “In this world of AI, we’ve essentially made the cost of perpetrating fraud $0,” says Scott.
Moreover, fraudsters usually arrive prepared, with stolen identity data in hand, says Scott. “The real customer is the one that gets stuck re-uploading the blurry photo of his or her license,” he says. He sees the most abandonment at the photo upload step and when applicants face one step-up check after another. “Once the applicant walks away, especially from a digital application, they rarely come back.”
Hal Lonas, chief technology officer at identity verification provider Trulioo, sees the same risk from the institution’s side. “I don’t want to hold them up too soon in the process because they might get disenfranchised and go away,” he says.
Adding checks doesn’t solve this. Many legacy fraud tools return one of three answers, approve, reject or try harder, says Sean McElroy, chief risk officer at Lumin Digital, which provides digital banking software to banks and credit unions. Each “try harder” passes the applicant to another tool. “Just piling up checkpoints sort of puts the burden on good customers without stopping much fraud,” says Scott. McElroy agrees. “As those technologies become better at fooling the front door, you don’t want to add more front doors,” he says.
Instant verification speeds up the front door and still checks who the applicant is. Lonas starts with device intelligence, which flags phones tied to known fraud, then matches the applicant’s name, date of birth and address against third-party and credit data. It takes seconds, and depending on how an institution is regulated, it can be enough to approve someone without a document.
On the account side, instant verification lets applicants link an existing account at another institution. “A lot of people are now thinking about, let’s put that at the very front, because it’s a very strong signal,” says McElroy. “You’re not asking them to do much more than maybe open their password manager and connect an account.”
The goal is an account opened by a legitimate person who funds it and keeps using it. Fraudulent accounts and abandoned applications both stand in the way, and instant checks help with each. They screen applicants early without slowing down genuine ones, and a linked account gives new customers an easy way to make their first deposit.
Post-approval, Institutions still need to confirm the customer is who they claim to be and learn how they use the account. Lonas recommends a document check later if a transaction tops $10,000 or the profile changes. Some institutions open the account right away but hold back riskier features, like small business invoicing, until the account shows signs of everyday use, says McElroy.
Two kinds of activity point to a legitimate customer. Direct deposit shows there’s an employer behind the account. Routine debit card purchases, like groceries, are the other telling sign, says McElroy.
Key insight: Instant checks get good applicants approved and funded quickly, but verification continues after that. Early direct deposits and card spending keep confirming the customer is legitimate, and that same activity turns a new account into an active one.
A verification step can post strong fraud scores and still cost an institution good customers. McElroy gives an example: an applicant whose phone can’t take a clear photo of their driver’s license gives up. That person never gets scored, so the document check records no false rejection and looks like it’s working. “Your metrics are way off, and you may not even know it,” says McElroy.
Scott measures verification on both sides. “The fraud loss here matters, but it’s only one part of the picture,” he says. He also tracks how many good applicants got flagged, where applicants walk away, how long it takes to clear someone who got flagged, complaints and calls to the branch, and accounts that never get funded. Those numbers show how many checks an institution can add before lost applicants cost more than the fraud the checks prevent.
At many institutions, those numbers sit with different teams. Fraud and compliance track how much fraud gets caught, and growth tracks completed and funded applications. Lonas says the two sides rarely talk regularly and often meet only when a problem arises.
The volume of attacks makes that split harder to manage. Institutions used to have time to review suspicious activity and staff to do it, says Scott. Now attacks come too fast for people to keep up. He says institutions need automated tools that can add a check, block an applicant or limit what an account can do within seconds, with an analyst making the final call. “AI can watch all the screens all the time, and all at once,” he says.
Key insight: A verification step costs an institution in two ways: fraud that gets through and good applicants who don’t. Both belong on one scorecard that fraud and growth teams read together.

articles.title_orig: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.title_zh: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.content_orig:
Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" in the Middle East and other areas, the US national intelligence director has warned in a memo seen by the BBC.
Jay Clayton's assessment come as the US State Department makes adjustments to staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, including the ordered departure earlier this week of non-emergency US embassy staff from Saudi Arabia.
The order came in response to escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia in the past month.
Clayton's memo was marked unclassified and sent to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.
It said: "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries."
Clayton said he was making every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it with US State Department personnel.
A US official told the BBC: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment.
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis say the attacks on Saudi Arabia are in retaliation to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport they blame on the kingdom.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks. Some 155 civilians have been killed in Yemen since, according to the Houthi-run health ministry.
This particular conflict has re-emerged on the backdrop of a wider conflict in the Middle East.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has seen oil prices surge, exacerbated by the Houthis' "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_zh: October 23, 2026 - Letters from an American | Heather Cox Richardson
articles.source: Letters from an American | Heather Cox Richardson
articles.content_orig:
Senior executives at a US liquefied natural gas company resigned after discovering that sanctioned Russian energy giant Novatek was allegedly financing and directing a $25 billion gas export project in Alaska, despite lacking the necessary US government authorization.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Financial Times on October 24, former Polar LNG chief executive Joel Riddle stepped down in September after learning that Novatek was allegedly influencing the company’s strategic decisions. Nearly the entire senior management team subsequently resigned.
The project, known as Polar Train, was designed to develop LNG export infrastructure on Alaska’s North Slope and supply Asian markets, supporting Washington’s ambitions to expand US energy exports.
The venture was initially associated with Gentry Beach, a longtime friend of Donald Trump Jr. who also served as a finance vice-chairman for President Donald Trump’s 2017 inauguration.
However, Riddle told the Financial Times that he later discovered Beach had not invested in the company and held no ownership or executive position. Instead, he alleged that funding was coming from Russian interests.
The project involved plans to repurpose partially completed LNG production equipment originally intended for Novatek’s Arctic LNG 2 facility in Siberia, which has been targeted by US sanctions.
According to The New York Times , internal correspondence indicated that Novatek executives, including chief executive Leonid Mikhelson, discussed providing up to $15 million in financing through UAE-based Tech Wave.
Novatek acknowledged an agreement allowing Tech Wave to use its technology in Alaska and confirmed signing a memorandum of understanding with Polar Train in April. The Russian company also told the New York Times that it intended to acquire a minority stake in the project.
The Financial Times reported that the proposed arrangement could have involved Novatek contributing technology and expertise in exchange for sanctions relief for Arctic LNG 2.
The negotiations reportedly extended beyond commercial discussions. According to the New York Times, cooperation involving Novatek was discussed in September between Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as part of broader talks aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Polar LNG rejected Riddle’s allegations, describing him as a disgruntled employee and maintaining that its operations complied with applicable laws. The company confirmed that it had sought US authorization to use Russian LNG equipment.
Earlier, Eric Trump moved forward with a luxury tower project in Georgia alongside developers allegedly linked to a sanctioned pro-Kremlin billionaire and a businessman previously investigated by the FBI over suspected ties to Russian organized crime.

articles.title_orig: Google illegally cut down 250K trees in Finland for data center, driving wolves into villages and infuriating locals: report
articles.title_zh: Google illegally cut down 250K trees in Finland for data center, driving wolves into villages and infuriating locals: report
articles.content_orig:
Google illegally demolished an estimated 250,000 trees in Finland to make way for a data center, leaving behind a lifeless mud wasteland that forced packs of wolves into a nearby town in search of food and infuriated locals, according to a report.
The tech super giant – continuing its expansion of the booming artificial intelligence industry – cleared 816 acres of woodlands in Northern Finland, The Guardian reported Thursday.
Google is accused of removing the trees and clearing the land before it had full approval — as Finnish law requires companies to complete a mandatory Environmental Impact Assessment before large-scale operations.
Finnish officials, outraged by the mass destruction, suspended all development at two of Google’s data center sites to assess the environmental impact.
The operation took place outside the rural town of Muhos — southeast of Finland’s fifth-largest city, Oulu — as devastating images of the aftermath captured the vast barren land filled only with tire tracks, muddy puddles and mounds of dirt.
The removal of the large area of trees destroyed the wildlife in the forest, leaving predators like wolves to search for food closer to human developments in the village of Otanmäki, 50 miles from the site.
“We had wolves coming into the village because all the wild animals moved out of the forest,” resident Anni Ranta told the Guardian.
“They fled. What worries me about the data centers is also the noise because this is hard rock soil. Even when we are standing here talking,” she added, comparing the sound to a drum.
Angry residents called out Google, asking for reprieve from the company to help repay for losses the community sustained from previous tech expansions on the land.
“It has been done in the wrong way. American style. No sense. No sense at all,” Muhos resident Antti Jakonen told the outlet, calling on the company to help restore the local salmon population that had been destroyed by hydropower years ago.
Ranta revealed she feared the construction of the data centers would be a perfect target for Russian aggression in the already tense European domain.
“I don’t want them in Finland at all. I don’t like the whole idea of AI and the world changing and the way it’s changing. It’s going too fast, too soon.”
Google’s two sites near Muhos and Kajaani, roughly 90 miles apart, are part of its $15 billion investment for AI infrastructure in the Nordic country, which was announced in September.
The Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency gave Google’s project subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, a deadline of Oct. 23 to suspend all operations
“In the opinion of the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority, extensive preparatory measures have already been taken in the project areas based on the currently available reports, such as the removal of trees, the stripping of topsoil, the construction of construction site roads and storage areas, changes to ditches and culverts, and stormwater arrangements,” Tommi Muilu, Head of the Environmental Department, said.
“In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure,” Muilu said.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
The removal of the trees led to water sources flowing near the site to turn brown and pollute the streams that feed the Oulujoki River.
Google’s Finnish top chief Antti Järvinen claimed the company believed it had legislative approval to commence the large-scale tree cutting.
Järvinen’s explanation was blasted as being “pure arrogance” from the trillion dollar Alphabet company.
“They bought the vast land area and they just started to cut it, just like that,” she said. “It’s pure arrogance and it’s amazing,” Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL) chair Hanna Halmeenpää said, according to the Guardian.
Opponents of the data center believe Google had been rushing to construct the complex before legislation in Finland caught up on AI advancements to implement regulations.
Järvinen apologized for the destruction as the company said it would work to protect water sources before planting back trees around 321 of the acres.
“I wonder why we have to sacrifice so much of our nature. They give everything away too easily,” conservationist Vesa Hyyryläinen told the outlet.
In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order, banning all large-scale AI data centers from the state, the first such ban in the US.
The executive order paused new permits for so-called “hyperscale” data centers that looked to use the Empire State’s electrical grid for up to a year.
“I don’t want New York to just be first. I want New York to be first in the right way,” Hochul said at the time.

articles.title_orig: How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
articles.title_zh: How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
articles.content_orig:
How Netanyahu reshaped Israel after 18 years in power
To his supporters, he is known as “King Bibi”; but to his opponents, he is the king of security failures and corruption.
Disputes over names aside, what is not in question is that Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has left his mark on the country’s institutions, politics and social attitudes during a decades-long career that has been defined by Israel’s lurch to the right.
As he seeks re-election in Israel’s October 27 polls, analysts say his most enduring domestic legacy may be the right-wing, militaristic opposition that he has helped create and now faces.
Born in 1949, Netanyahu entered Israel’s central political stage in the early 1990s by fuelling anger at possible peace deals with the Palestinians and Syria.
Israeli political leaders have accused him of leading incitement that motivated the 1995 assassination of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who was leading negotiations with the Palestine Liberation Organization, by an ultranationalist Israeli. Netanyahu had led rallies in which participants depicted Rabin in a Nazi SS uniform and held signs of him in the crosshairs of a gun, while others shouted “traitor”.
The Likud Party leader denies any responsibility, but former security officials have said they warned Netanyahu before the assassination and asked him to dial down his rhetoric, only for him to refuse, according to Israeli media reports.
In 1996, Netanyahu’s populist tactics succeeded at the ballot box, making him Israel’s youngest prime minister. Netanyahu’s transactional leadership style gave prominence to extreme-right and religious parties that are now an indispensable part of his right-wing alliance.
Under him, religious courts have expanded powers, including over civil and business disputes. State institutions accommodate religious agendas and allocate record levels of funding to ultra-Orthodox schools and institutions.
Netanyahu inscribed his political ideology, especially on the identity of the state and the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel, into law. In 2018, the Knesset passed the so-called Nation-State Basic Law , which states – among other things – that Israel is the exclusive state of the Jewish people and also makes advancing illegal settlements a national priority.
Human rights organisations in Israel petitioned the High Court to stop the legislation from going into effect, but the petition was rejected. International experts and rights groups cite this law, among others, as evidence of Israel committing the crime of apartheid in its treatment of Palestinians.
Netanyahu also re-engineered state institutions, including Israel’s security structures, appointing loyalists and political allies to senior positions. He also clashed with security chiefs that he deemed antagonistic. And in the aftermath of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, which triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, Netanyahu deflected blame and responsibility on the security establishment, prompting Ronen Bar, who was the Shin Bet chief in 2023, to sue him for defamation.
A major change to Israeli institutions that was spearheaded by Netanyahu during his 19 on-and-off years in power affected the judiciary, which is examining lingering corruption charges that could see him serve time in prison if he is convicted. Netanyahu, who is up against three separate cases of corruption filed in 2019, denies any wrongdoing.
Under his leadership, the Knesset adopted legislation that changed the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee to ensure greater political influence for the governing coalition.
Netanyahu called it “judicial reform” to stop what he often calls a “judicial dictatorship” ruling over elected officials.
Opponents called it a “coup” that sparked wide-scale protests : a push to curtail the independence of the High Court and give politicians influence over the courts and ministerial legal advisers.
In line with his efforts to subvert independent oversight, Netanyahu tried repeatedly, but unsuccessfully, to fire the attorney general.
But he succeeded in dismissing the military’s advocate general for leaking a video of Israeli soldiers gang-raping a Palestinian detainee. The soldiers were also released and cleared of charges.
At the same time, Netanyahu is dogged by corruption cases dating back to 2019, which could see him serve time in prison if convicted
The prime minister, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza, says his work is not over. He promises his supporters he will complete the overhaul of judicial review and press on with other highly controversial policies.
Netanyahu’s supporters and allies view him as a leader who delivers, and one who achieved what others could not. His opponents pledge to undo the damage Netanyahu caused over the past decades, pointing to corruption, social divisions and increasing international isolation as outcomes of his rule.
But undoing such formative changes, many of which are now law, may be easier said than done.

articles.title_orig: Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege
articles.title_zh: Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege
articles.content_orig:
Taiz, Yemen – It was approaching 10:30am in the dialysis centre of the Republican Hospital in Taiz when a machine began filtering excess fluids, toxins and salts from the blood of Omar Mukhtar Hammoud.
The 16-year-old suffers from kidney failure and is one of 270 patients who regularly receive dialysis at the centre in the government-held city in southwest Yemen. But with essential medical supplies and fuel running critically low under the renewed Houthi siege , doctors fear they may soon be unable to provide the treatment that keeps their patients alive.
Dr Essam Mahyoub Dahan, the centre’s director, warned that a complete shutdown could happen within days.
“Because of the siege and the shortage of diesel and medical solutions, we have recently been forced to reduce dialysis sessions from four hours to just two and a half,” Dahan told Al Jazeera. “We know this is not adequate, but we have no choice if we are to keep the centre operating for as long as possible before it shuts down completely.”
Dahan said the centre’s remaining stocks of specialised dialysis solutions were also close to running out.
The supplies, which are expensive, are normally provided by the Yemeni Ministry of Health every three months. But the latest delivery which was due earlier this month  failed to arrive because of the Houthi siege on Taiz city. It began in the first week of October after Houthi advances in the Taiz countryside.
The city was previously under complete Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, in the early years of Yemen’s ongoing war.
Across Taiz governorate, where battles are raging between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iranian-allied Houthi fighters, the number of patients at risk is far greater.
In an October 12 statement, the governorate’s health office warned that the continued siege and obstruction of essential supplies could endanger the lives of 1,110 patients with kidney failure. They depend on dialysis services in the governorate’s hospitals, which collectively provide about 210 dialysis sessions a day.
International humanitarian and health organisations have issued similar warnings about the impact of the siege on the already fragile healthcare system in Taiz.
On Thursday, Amnesty International called on the Houthis to immediately reopen vital roads into and around the city, warning that the closure of the main road between Taiz and the southern port city of Aden threatened hundreds of thousands of civilians with losing access to food, water and healthcare.
Taiz’s hospitals depend heavily on diesel-powered generators because much of the city’s electricity infrastructure was destroyed during the war that began 11 years ago and has not been restored.
The renewed Houthi siege has severely disrupted the entry of fuel, including the diesel needed to run hospital generators and lifesaving medical equipment.
Dr Shaheed al-Ameri, deputy director-general for technical affairs at the Republican Hospital, said the shortages have had a devastating impact on medical services.
“A very large part of this suffering is because of the shortage of diesel,” he told Al Jazeera. “We have no reserve diesel supplies. Our stocks ran out early in the siege and we are now buying it on the black market almost every day, at prices that have reached five times what they were before the siege.”
Al-Ameri warned that the longer the siege continues, the more prices will rise and the further medical services will deteriorate.
The hospital has already suspended operations in some departments, including essential units, he said.
“If this situation continues much longer, we fear we will reach a complete and comprehensive collapse of healthcare services,” he said.
The shortages are not confined to the Republican Hospital. On October 22, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies were threatening lifesaving healthcare throughout  Taiz governorate, with some hospital services already disrupted.
According to the WHO, 42 health facilities in Taiz city had reported severe shortages of essential supplies. Hospitals and ambulances require at least 156,000 litres of fuel a month to continue functioning.
The organisation also warned that diesel shortages threaten to disrupt oxygen production, water pumping, vaccine refrigeration and sanitation services, increasing the risks of disease outbreaks, particularly among displaced families and other vulnerable groups.
The United Nations has separately warned that the restrictions on supplies are bringing Taiz’s health system close to collapse and urged the Houthis to allow humanitarian assistance and essential goods to enter without obstruction.
In its October 12 statement, Taiz’s health office warned that continued restrictions on fuel deliveries could lead to the shutdown of medical oxygen production plants, further endangering patients.
Taysir al-Samei, the health office’s media officer, said that would dramatically worsen the crisis.
“Many medical departments depend on oxygen, particularly operating theatres, inpatient wards, intensive care units and incubators for premature babies,” al-Samei said.
“Most hospitals have already suspended services in some units because of the shortage of diesel and the lack of necessary medical solutions, as well as shortages of medical staff who are struggling to get to work because of the lack of transport,” he added.
He warned that if conditions continued to deteriorate at the same pace, some hospitals could stop providing services in the coming days.
At the Republican Hospital, al-Ameri said that shortages were also affecting diagnostics and treatment. The availability of laboratory reagents had fallen to just 10 to 15 percent of previous levels, he said, while approximately half of the medicines normally available were now out of stock.
Prices for the remaining medicines had doubled, he said, placing them further out of reach for patients already struggling with Yemen’s worsening economic crisis.
The continued fighting and shelling around Taiz have increased the number of wounded people requiring emergency care – placing additional pressure on facilities already struggling with shortages of surgical supplies , anaesthetics and intravenous fluids.
Abdul Badi Abdulwuhab, 53, is another dialysis patient in the Republican Hospital, struggling to cope with the shorter dialysis sessions.
His voice was filled with desperation.
“Because of these measures, I suffer from weakness and I cannot bear the pain,” Abdul Badi told Al Jazeera. “Two and a half hours is not enough to remove all the fluids and toxins from my body.”
Dr Dahan said that the patient’s condition had deteriorated since his sessions were shortened.
“These measures are not effective for many patients,” Dahan said. “The only solution is to end the siege and return things to the way they were.”

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu Has Reinvented Himself. Will Voters Think It’s Enough?
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu Has Reinvented Himself. Will Voters Think It’s Enough?
articles.content_orig:
Yoram Ariely left Israel more than thirty years ago and found his way to New York City, where he worked in the food-and-beverage industry. “Mostly juices,” he told me. He eventually retired to Florida, but on Wednesday he was back in New York, sitting in the departures terminal at Kennedy Airport. Ariely is eighty-four years old; when I approached him, he requested that I give him a moment so he could put in his hearing aids. His journey, which had begun that morning, at 7 A.M. , in Sarasota, would end up totalling twenty-four hours. He already looked exhausted.
Ariely, along with others clustered around Gate 18B, waiting to board a non-stop flight to Tel Aviv, was returning to Israel to cast a ballot in the country’s upcoming election—the first time Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will face voters since his contentious effort to neuter Israel’s judiciary; his failure to prevent the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023; and his prosecution of the ensuing war on Gaza, which has shredded Israel’s international reputation and resulted in a warrant for his arrest, for war crimes, from The Hague. “This is the most important election of my lifetime,” Ariely said. (Given that he’s six years older than the Israeli state, his lifetime includes every previous Israeli election.) It will be the first time he’s voted in Israel since moving away.
Around eleven per cent of the Israeli electorate lives abroad. The country does not permit absentee voting, except in rare cases, so any citizen who wants to cast a ballot must return and, on election day, go to the designated polling place for their last official in-country address. This puts a huge price, in time and money—often hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars—on casting a single vote. For Ariely and many like him, it is no deterrent. Eight in ten Israeli voters who live abroad share his view that the upcoming election is “the most crucial” in Israel’s history. Polls show Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition in a dead heat with his chief rival, the centrist Gadi Eisenkot .
Ariely is to the left of Eisenkot politically, but “these considerations must be put aside to give him the majority,” he told me. A man named Hiam Simon, a Jewish American dual citizen who lived in Israel for a stretch in the seventies, piped up from the row of seats opposite us. Ariely, he said, should throw his lot in with the Democrats, a smaller party that would likely become part of Eisenkot’s government, so as to “pull the coalition to the left.”
Ariely was booked in a block of coach seats that had been reserved by the America-Israel Democracy ( AID ) Coalition, a nonprofit based in Pennsylvania that seeks to mobilize Israeli citizens and “concerned Americans” in “preserving the democratic foundations of the state of Israel.” (Simon bought his own ticket, in business class, on the same flight.) The AID Coalition was formed in 2023, after Netanyahu proposed that the Knesset, by majority vote, should be able to overrule Supreme Court decisions. That move sparked enormous street protests in Israel, and alarmed many Israeli citizens overseas.
When the election date was set, this past July—spurred by the legal mandate that Israel hold a parliamentary election at least every four years—the war that Israel and the U.S. had launched against Iran was in its fifth month. Many foreign airlines had paused service to Israel. On those airlines that hadn’t, prices were steep; in May, a round-trip coach seat on our route from New York was running as high as twenty-five hundred dollars. The AID Coalition launched an initiative, Fly&Vote, to help people get back to cast their ballots.
Officially, AID is nonpartisan and assists any eligible voter, irrespective of their political leanings. “We don’t ask,” Batell Blaish-Sultanik, the group’s executive director, told me. Under Israeli election law, it is illegal to provide free or subsidized trips. AID bought blocks of seats on Arkia Israeli Airlines at a commercial rate, securing around a hundred seats on each of five inbound flights before the election and five outbound flights after it. Tickets were then sold to voters at set prices at the lower end of the market rate—topping out at nine hundred dollars each way. Hagai Nassau, an environmental consultant in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, who left Israel as a five-year-old and now sports a graying beard, told me that he had glanced at flights on El Al “and it was, like, three thousand bucks. So I was, like, I’ll do Fly&Vote.”
Of course, for some overseas Israeli citizens, price is no object. Soon after chatting with Nassau at our gate, I spotted Neri Oxman, an Israeli-born architect and the wife of the hedge-fund billionaire Bill Ackman, by a barista counter in the Centurion Lounge. Ackman was sitting nearby. Oxman told me that she saw no option but to return for this election. “It’s so important,” she said, stiffening up like a soldier. “I’m doing my civic duty.” They would be flying El Al.
More than thirty-five thousand overseas Israeli citizens registered to receive information about the AID Coalition’s reserved seats, and for access to a bespoke search engine that had been programmed to find other, affordable options, with complicated itineraries and long layovers. AID estimates that more than sixty thousand will ultimately vote on October 27th.
Netanyahu’s Likud Party clearly regards overseas voters as an obstacle—perhaps even an enemy. While there is scant survey data on the political leanings of Israelis who live abroad, they tend to be secular and more educated, and it is assumed that they skew anti-Netanyahu. More than a quarter of a million people have left the country since 2023. In August, Likud’s attorneys accused the AID Coalition of bribing voters, and brought legal action to try to block its efforts. Three weeks before the election, the chairman of Israel’s Central Elections Committee dismissed the case, but the AID Coalition agreed not to buy more blocks on additional flights. Over the summer, anonymous sources inside Israel’s Transportation Ministry, which is helmed by the populist Likud provocateur Miri Regev, leaked to Israeli media that officials were plotting to reduce capacity at the country’s only major international airport in order to stop anti-Likud voters from arriving. (The AID Coalition has distributed the phone numbers of attorneys to call if any of its passengers run into trouble at passport control.)
Besides the Fly&Vote initiative, several other efforts to bring in voters seem to be under way. A group called Mind-IL is running something called Israeli Science and Academia Week—fifty-nine scholarly conferences, ranging in topics from A.I. to zoology, which all conclude the day before the election. Organizers expect to draw well over three thousand participants, many from overseas. Guli Dolev-Hashiloni, an Israeli-born scholar and activist who is flying in from Berlin, where he is a Ph.D. student in Jewish history, categorized the conferences as “a very good subversive act of Israeli academia that enables people to come back to vote without taking vacation days.” Ran I. Snitkovsky, a member of Mind-IL’s steering committee and a professor at the business school of Tel Aviv University, insisted that any intimation that he and his colleagues were gaming the electoral system was unfair. “We realized there will be a lot of people that want to be here, and we wanted to take advantage of that,” Snitkovsky told me. The result, whatever the intention, will be hundreds of foreign-based academics flying to Israel the week of the election, many on stipends from their universities. Meital Avivi-Reich, an Israeli-born expert on the science of speech perception, who teaches at CUNY , applied for fifteen hundred dollars in funding to present her research at one of the Mind-IL conferences. That will help with the airfare, she told me, but she still plans to stay with her mother and then crash with friends during her shoestring voting-cum-conference

articles.title_orig: France is looking ungovernable. And it’s going to get worse
articles.title_zh: France is looking ungovernable. And it’s going to get worse
articles.content_orig:
The kids are not alright. Across Europe, young people are protesting issues ranging from a lack of funding for education to the cost of housing, posing massive challenges to governments already under pressure and providing a visible sign of the intergenerational frustration felt by Gen Z.
The precise configuration of these grievances varies from country to country. In Spain , the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her home served as the catalyst for this wave of protests; in France, it was students demonstrating in support of striking teachers; student protests have rocked Albania on and off for months, first sparked by plans for a luxury development backed by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Despite their different catalysts, however, all these movements have acted as a sort of black hole, drawing in any discontent before exploding in a catch-all outburst of frustration for a generation of young people who fear they won’t have the same opportunities as their parents. They have, in part, inspired each other, too. Protesters in Italy and Greece have referenced their French counterparts in their slogans. Housing protests in Spain spilled over into Portugal. And student unions across Europe are sharing advice and their experiences with one another, Alice de Brito, vice president of France’s main student union, UNEF, told CNN.
“I see so many more similarities than differences,” she said. “We are all talking about the need for investments in education, in the universities, in youth in general. But we are also talking about the cost of living, about housing.”
That echoes the demands made by Italian student union leader Sabrina Brizzola, who told a rally last weekend: “Let’s… make ourselves heard for schools that don’t collapse on our heads, for safe and dignified work, for public healthcare, for social justice.”
For Julius Fintelmann, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of the European Correspondent daily newsletter, the protests “reflect a kind of frustration, the feeling that Europe’s politics is failing to deliver for the next generation.”
As well as education and housing, he points to an increasingly uncertain job market, where artificial intelligence disproportionately affects entry-level jobs, and the climate crisis as laying the groundwork for this explosion of Gen Z anger. “I think fundamentally what we see is this promise that liberal democracy had, which was that the next generation will enjoy a better life than the current one, that promise simply doesn’t hold true anymore,” he told CNN.
And the European Union countries most affected by protests – Greece, Italy, France, Belgium, Spain and Portugal – share a gloomy economic backdrop and high levels of national debt, making it hard to increase public spending. Bond yields in France, for example, ticked up to their highest levels since 2002 on Wednesday, exerting more pressure on government budgets.
Student protests like this have been held at the start of the French school year in September and October for the past nine years as young people returning to education realize they don’t have enough teachers or good equipment, noted de Brito.
This year, however, they snowballed, as students demanded reduced class sizes, increased spending on teachers, investment in infrastructure to withstand the climate crisis and an end to police violence against young people. “People are just tired of waiting for an answer,” de Brito said.
Education is a theme that cuts across Europe’s borders. Thousands of students and teachers marched across Greece, including a group who gathered outside parliament in Athens chanting, “from Greece to France, we want public, free education,” according to Reuters. When students first occupied a high school in Rome, on October 7, they wrote “like in France” in the first line of the statement defending their actions.
The Italian government has sought to downplay any similarities with the protest movement in France. “The situation in Italy is very different from France,” Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said earlier this month, repeating a far-right claim that the French protests are fueled by the difficulty, absent in Italy, of integrating second-generation migrants into the school system.
Nonetheless, housing is another issue that cuts across national borders. Italian protesters say they have closely watched housing protests in Spain, which erupted in earnest in September and ultimately forced the government to call snap elections.
Students at a protest camp in Rome told CNN that affordable housing was inseparable from a good education. One, Elisa Pastore, said she and her brother can “barely” afford the rent for their shared room in the Italian capital, where they attend university. For the first half of her degree, before her brother started university too, she had to commute 120 kilometers (75 miles) from outside Rome in order to save money.
Other groups are protesting, too. A blockade by truckers in Italy, outraged by the rising cost of fuel following the Iran war, has halted production of buffalo mozzarella and some pasta. And issues like housing transcend generational divides, drawing older generations into the protests as well.
In Portugal, thousands of people have gathered in Rossio Square, one of Lisbon’s busiest plazas, every evening this week. Some even pitched tents and 55 people were arrested in the early hours of Tuesday morning, prompting further demonstrations. Protesters, waving flags with slogans like “Casas para morar,” meaning “Homes to live in,” have demanded caps on rent hikes and the reversal of a new law that would make evictions easier.
Elsewhere, long-running demonstrations in Albania and Serbia have focused more on anti-corruption, spiraling into movements seeking to topple each country’s government.
After the protests in Albania turned violent last week, Prime Minister Edi Rama resisted any calls to step down, instead accusing protesters of threatening his plans for the country to join the EU and blaming his political opponents for the unrest.
“We want a change, that’s why we’re here,” one protester in Albania told Reuters. “We want a revolution, we want a new government, we are not looking for any negotiations, we need a new government as soon as possible.”
Meanwhile in Serbia, the student-led protests that have shaped the country’s politics for the past two years now form the most formidable opposition to longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in parliamentary elections on Sunday.
More demonstrations are on the way. France is bracing for yet another wave of protests, with authorities racing to prevent a repeat of the kind of public disorder seen last weekend. A large demonstration is set to take place in Paris on Saturday afternoon, organized by France’s main student uion, UNEF, with one of the country’s biggest trade unions, CGT, announcing it will join. Other groups are expected to attend, including farmers, climate activists and the Yellow Vests, the movement that first emerged in 2018 during the protests over fuel costs.
While the protest in Paris has been authorized by the authorities, French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday banned all non-trade union protests on Saturday as he seeks to control the civil unrest. Nonetheless, widespread demonstrations are expected in Orléans, where hard-right figurehead Marine Le Pen launches her presidential campaign this weekend.
Major trade unions in France and Spain have called for a general strike on November 5 and 11, respectively. In Germany, a group calling itself “Gen Z regelt” (“Gen Z’s got it”) has called for nationwide protests on October 31. And student unions in Britain and Italy are planning a day of action on November 20 to protest the rising cost of education.
CNN’s Stefano Pozzebon, Pierre Bairin, Lucie Lepellec and Will Ripley contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: China carries out in-depth investigation of Turkey’s largest rare earth deposit
articles.content_orig:
New study sheds light on how rare earth elements built up in carbonatite-related formations at the Kizilcaoren deposit
Although the findings shed light on how rare earth elements accumulate in carbonatite-related formations, the researchers concluded that the site was unlikely to emerge as a major global alternative to existing producers any time soon.
Lead scientist Professor Yang Xiaoyong noted that the deposit’s mineralisation was “small in scale” and “still far from reaching the large scale of rare earth deposits”. The findings point to the steep geological and economic barriers nations face as they attempt to diversify their sources of critical minerals.

articles.title_orig: El Salvador sends special forces to search for troops missing in Haiti
articles.title_zh: El Salvador sends special forces to search for troops missing in Haiti
articles.content_orig:
El Salvador has deployed troops to Haiti to try to rescue four Salvadoran service members believed to have been captured by Haitian gangs, according to a spokesperson for the UN-authorized multinational security mission in Haiti known as the Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The missing service members, described as non-combatant aviation technicians that were supporting the GSF mission, were ambushed by gangs on October 18, Salvadoran officials have said.
The GSF has been carrying out a dayslong operation to try to find them. The effort has resulted in armed clashes that have left at least seven gang members dead and four GSF personnel wounded, the GSF has said.
A spokesperson for the security mission confirmed to CNN on Thursday Salvadoran troops had arrived in Haiti to support the effort.
The Miami Herald first reported that a 100-strong team was deployed. El Salvador has not commented on the specific details of the mission.
It comes a day after Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele announced that his country had launched an unspecified “military operation” to rescue the missing men.
Can hired mercenaries succeed where others have failed?
Bukele, who has carried out a brutal crackdown on gangs in his own country, warned Haitian gang members that they would face a more severe response if they didn’t release the service members alive.
“And do not take our word for empty threats. We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too,” he said on X.
Gang leader Lanmo Sanjou issued a response to Bukele on Thursday, filming himself with large quantities of ammunition and warning that his group would “fight to stay alive.”
The GSF was established by the UN Security Council in 2025 to help Haiti fight the gangs plaguing the country . According to the resolution adopted at that time, the force consists of 5,500 military or police personnel and 50 civilians from various nations. El Salvador is one of the countries that agreed to provide personnel. Bukele says their primary job is to carry out medical evacuations.
CNN’s Mauricio Torres contributed to this report.
