articles.title_orig: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 23, 2026
articles.title_zh: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 23, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
Ukrainian officials are widely reporting continued in-motion speed restrictions on SpaceX’s low-earth orbit satellite communication technology (Starlink and Starshield) on October 23, but the situation remains unclear. Ukrainian sources, including the Ukrainian General Staff and sources within the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (MoD), reported on October 23 that Ukrainian forces have observed “cases of connection loss” in Starlink/Starshield terminal operations at speeds of 161 kilometers per hour (around 100 miles per hour).[1] Sources within the Ukrainian MoD stated that there has been “no confirmation” about the removal of in-motion speed restrictions.[2] Ukrainian defense minister Serhii Sternenko stated that the situation with Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions “remains ambiguous” since some Ukrainian units report the resumption of operations at speeds exceeding the previously established limits, but the resumption does not apply to all missions, and he noted that some disruptions continue.[3] The situation regarding in-motion Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions remains unclear, but Ukrainian sources are emphasizing that Ukrainian forces continue experiencing problems with accessing Starlink/Starshield terminals as of October 23.
Russia and Ukraine have reportedly agreed to a limited ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast. The White House reported on October 23 that US First Lady Melania Trump secured a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in Russia-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast beginning on October 29 to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation from the city amid a dire humanitarian crisis.[4] Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on October 23 the White House’s press release and noted that Ukraine and Russia agreed to conduct a humanitarian mission in occupied Oleshky, including securing a limited ceasefire, delivering humanitarian cargo to the city, and ensuring the free movement of civilians from the settlement.[5] Russian Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov confirmed on October 23 that Russia agreed to the limited ceasefire in the Kherson direction beginning at 0400 local Moscow time on October 27 — a notably different start date from the one given in the White House press release.[6]
Russian occupation authorities are fully responsible for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky and have repeatedly and deliberately blocked evacuation and humanitarian routes into the settlement since the beginning of Russia’s occupation.[7] Russian occupation authorities stopped the delivery of food and other critical supplies into Oleshky in late December 2025 and have failed to deliver any food or medicine to Oleshky since May 2026. The Kremlin rejected three local humanitarian ceasefire proposals from Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets in May, July, and September 2026, after which Ukrainian forces conducted an operation to provide food to Oleshky residents via drone drops in September 2026.[8] Russian authorities have long refused to address the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, and Gerasimov’s October 23 statement is the first instance of a Russian attempt to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries.
Russian President Vladimir Putin articulated his long-standing commitment to wider territorial aims in Ukraine far beyond Donetsk Oblast by invoking mythologized and false Russian “historical claims”. Putin claimed on October 22 that occupied Ukraine is “the territory of historical Russia” while rejecting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s October 21 proposal to freeze the current frontline as part of a ceasefire agreement.[9] Putin also claimed that the “latest genetic research” identifies Russians and Ukrainians as “one people.” Putin’s October 22 reference to “historical Russia” likely refers to “Novorossiya” — an amorphous invented region in southern and eastern Ukraine that the Kremlin has claimed is “integral” to Russia.[10] Novorossiya notably includes not only Crimea and the four oblasts that Russia has illegally annexed (Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts), but also Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa oblasts.[11] Putin’s invocation of Russia’s historical claims demands that Ukraine surrender the Ukrainian-controlled 20.5 percent of Donetsk Oblast, 24.5 percent of Zaporizhia Oblast, including Zaporizhzhia City with a pre-war population of over 700,000 people, and 30 percent of Kherson Oblast, including Kherson City with a pre-war population of nearly 300,000 people. Putin’s October 23 statement explicitly demonstrates that Russian demands extend far beyond Ukraine’s Fortress Belt and Donetsk Oblast and may include the entire territory of Ukraine . Putin also emphasized his commitment to achieving all Russian war goals, which include the Russian demand for Ukraine’s full capitulation.[12] Putin’s statement demonstrates that the Kremlin is willing to participate in “negotiations” with Ukraine solely for the purpose of accepting Kyiv’s surrender — not for the purpose of coming to some compromise peace agreement.
Putin also agreed to discuss the “European security architecture as a whole” after ensuring Ukraine’s and Russia’s future security.[13] Putin’s comment on “revising” the European security architecture refers to another Russian long-standing demand first articulated in the December 2021 ultimatum preceding the full-scale invasion that includes halting the deployment of military forces and weapons systems to NATO states that joined the alliance after 1997 and granting Russia a veto over certain NATO exercises.[14] Putin’s December 2021 demands are incompatible with US President Donald Trump’s commitment to maintaining a US military presence in Poland and the current US troop deployments in the Baltic States.
The Kremlin appears to be increasingly adopting a more cautious monetary policy amid continued inflationary pressures, which may pose risks to wage growth and Russia’s defense industrial base (DIB). The Russian Central Bank announced on October 23 that it would keep the key interest rate at 14 percent for the second consecutive month, after lowering the rate 10 times over the past 18 months, citing elevated price pressure and high inflation expectations.[15] The Central Bank’s baseline scenario assumes an average key interest rate of 12.5 to 13.5 percent in 2027 — only 0.5 to 1.5 percentage points below the current rate. The Central Bank noted that underlying price growth is “not slowing” and identified pro-inflationary risks (or risk factors that increase inflation over the medium term), including price growth between five and six percent and estimated annual inflation of 6.8 percent. The Central Bank estimated that annual inflation will range between 7.1 and 7.6 percent by the end of 2026, a slight increase from the Central Bank’s September 11 announcement, and noted that volatile items like motor fuel (an oblique reference to the effects of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure) will continue impacting price dynamics. Russian Central Bank Chairwoman Elvira Nabiullina stated on October 23 that supply and demand continue facing inflationary risks, elevated inflation expectations, labor market tensions, and a larger budget deficit.[16] Nabiullina stated that Russia has experienced a decrease in consumer activity and that Russia’s GDP growth estimates for 2026 are between 0.5 and one percent. Nabiullina stated that the Central Bank is aiming to return the inflation rate to four percent in 2027.
The Russian Central Bank’s continued reduction of the key interest rate over an 18-month period prior to September 2026 likely contributed to domestic inflationary pressures.[17] Nabiullina has consistently expressed the need for monetary restraint — often trying to resist the Kremlin’s demands to expand capital availability for the Russian DIB and devalue the ruble to increase

articles.title_orig: Iran Plots, Houthi Attacks Spur US Departure Orders in Mideast
articles.title_zh: Iran Plots, Houthi Attacks Spur US Departure Orders in Mideast
articles.content_orig:
Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" in the Middle East and other areas, the US national intelligence director has warned in a memo seen by the BBC.
Jay Clayton's assessment come as the US State Department makes adjustments to staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, including the ordered departure earlier this week of non-emergency US embassy staff from Saudi Arabia.
The order came in response to escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia in the past month.
Clayton's memo was marked unclassified and sent to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.
It said: "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries."
Clayton said he was making every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it with US State Department personnel.
A US official told the BBC: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment.
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis say the attacks on Saudi Arabia are in retaliation to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport they blame on the kingdom.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks. Some 155 civilians have been killed in Yemen since, according to the Houthi-run health ministry.
This particular conflict has re-emerged on the backdrop of a wider conflict in the Middle East.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has seen oil prices surge, exacerbated by the Houthis' "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | JetBlue Creditors Hire Advisers as Airline’s Shares, Bonds Sink
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | JetBlue Creditors Hire Advisers as Airline’s Shares, Bonds Sink
articles.content_orig:
A group of JetBlue's major creditors has hired restructuring advisers after the airline's shares hit record lows, raising questions about how the carrier will manage its debt while trying to return to profitability. According to The Wall Street Journal , the creditors have brought in financial adviser PJT Partners and law firm Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld, citing people familiar with the matter.
The move follows a difficult year for JetBlue , which reportedly explored a potential sale to rivals, including United Airlines . The appointment of restructuring advisers does not mean bankruptcy or major operational changes are imminent, but it adds to growing concerns about the carrier's struggling financial position.
The creditor group includes holders of JetBlue's $2 billion in bonds due in 2031 and a $742 million first-lien loan. The New York-based carrier's stock dropped nearly 10% on Thursday to close at $2.65, its lowest level since it went public in 2002. In fact, its shares have plummeted by 42% so far this year amid a sharp rise in jet fuel prices.
JetBlue has spent the past two years trying to improve its performance through JetForward, a plan launched in July 2024 under CEO Joanna Geraghty. This focuses on controlling costs and making better use of the airline's network and aircraft. While the airline has made progress, higher operating costs have made a sustained recovery more difficult.
JetBlue recorded a $247 million net loss in the second quarter, even as revenue increased 14.5% year-on-year to $2.7 billion. In a statement to Reuters , JetBlue said it " remains confident in its JetForward strategy " and pointed to progress toward achieving sustained profitability.
Reports also emerged earlier this year that JetBlue had explored a possible sale to another airline , with United, Alaska Airlines and Southwest Airlines named as potential buyers. United CEO Scott Kirby was asked about JetBlue during a recent earnings call, but said he had " nothing new to add on that ."
Rising fuel prices have become a significant problem for airlines globally. US jet fuel prices have nearly doubled since late February, with JetBlue's average fuel price skyrocketing by 76% to $4.23 per gallon in the second quarter. Additionally, the airline raised its estimate for third-quarter fuel costs in September.
Like most major US airlines, JetBlue does not hedge a significant amount of its fuel, leaving it exposed to sudden price increases. As of June 30, the airline had $8.5 billion in debt and finance lease obligations, while S&P Global Ratings recently downgraded the airline, citing pressure from higher fuel prices.
JetBlue's third-quarter results on October 27 could offer clues about whether its turnaround is progressing quickly enough to reassure lenders and investors. Meanwhile, for passengers, there is no indication that JetBlue's current flight schedule or onboard offerings will change.
Despite the financial pressure, JetBlue continues to invest in its product and network as it looks to attract more passengers and increase revenue per flight. One of its most significant moves is the introduction of BlueFirst, a new domestic first-class cabin on flights that do not feature its Mint business-class product.
Earlier this month, the carrier opened bookings for BlueFirst on more than 30 routes, with the first service scheduled between Boston Logan (BOS) and Fort Lauderdale (FLL) on December 8. Among the perks of the new cabin are wider recliner seats, complimentary meals, premium snacks and drinks, and priority services.
The carrier is also strengthening its network at key airports. This includes Fort Lauderdale — where it increased capacity by nearly 40% after Spirit Airlines folded — and at its bases in New York and Boston. However, the carrier has deferred 44 Airbus A321neo deliveries to 2030 and beyond as it seeks to preserve cash while continuing its turnaround efforts.

articles.title_orig: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
articles.title_zh: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
articles.content_orig:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

articles.title_orig: US is reducing staffing at 4 Middle East embassies over increased threats from Iran
articles.title_zh: US is reducing staffing at 4 Middle East embassies over increased threats from Iran
articles.content_orig:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East , and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people , including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

articles.content_orig:
High-level representatives from the US and Russia discussed lifting sanctions against Russia's flagship Arctic LNG-2 project in exchange for Novatek's participation in a $25 billion US gas project in Alaska, according to the Financial Times .
Joel Riddle, former CEO of Polar Train LNG, stated that the Russian company Novatek had financed the Alaska gas terminal project and determined its strategic direction even before obtaining the necessary permits from US authorities.
According to him, he left the company in September due to concerns about violating sanctions. Nearly the entire management team, including the CFO, subsequently resigned.
The FT reviewed correspondence in which a top Novatek executive discussed project financing and expediting fund transfers. ​ According to the agency's sources, the project was part of negotiations between Washington and Moscow regarding potential business agreements amid attempts to end the war against Ukraine.
Discussions centered on Novatek's assistance in building the terminal in Alaska in exchange for lifting sanctions on Russia's Arctic LNG-2.
The project was launched with the participation of investor Gentry Beach, who is connected to the Trump family. Following Riddle's departure, Tim Talkington, the former head of Goldman Sachs' Russian division, became acting CEO.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin reached an agreement on the supply of Russian diesel fuel to the global market, signaling a partial lifting of sanctions against Russia.

articles.title_orig: Argentinian judge drops fraud investigation into Milei over crypto scandal
articles.title_zh: Argentinian judge drops fraud investigation into Milei over crypto scandal
articles.content_orig:
An Argentinian federal judge has dropped a criminal investigation into President Javier Milei and his sister Karina Milei over the collapse of a cryptocurrency he promoted online.
Judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi issued the decision on Friday, according to court records, ending an inquiry into Milei’s role in the launch of the $Libra token, which crashed after a brief rally.
“The reported events do not constitute a criminal offence,” the judge said in a ruling. He also wrote that investor losses and the rise and fall in the currency’s price were insufficient to establish fraud.
In his ruling, Martinez de Giorgi said that Milei’s institutional standing could have given the launch “greater impact” when he posted about it, but that does not translate into a fraudulent scheme.
Javier Milei recommended the little-known meme coin in a post on X in February 2025. He later deleted the post and denied any link to the cryptocurrency, whose value soon plunged.
The judge also dismissed an investigation into US businessman Hayden Davis, who described himself as a “launch adviser” for the token. Davis has acknowledged that he held close to $100m after the crash and denies any wrongdoing.
“For the first time in history, a President of the Nation was investigated with complete freedom, resulting in absolute proof of his innocence,” read a post shared on X by the official presidential office.
“The question that remains is this: Who will take responsibility for having wasted Argentine taxpayers’ money and the President of the Nation’s time in a failed attempt at an institutional coup?”
Milei is one of US President Donald Trump’s closest allies. Trump firmly backed him a year ago and has called him his “favourite president”.
Trump made clear the support hinged on a victory for Milei’s party.
“I’m with this man because his philosophy is correct,” he said ahead of a White House lunch with the Argentinian leader last year. “If he wins, we’re staying with him. And if he doesn’t win, we’re gone.”
Earlier this month, Milei urged Trump to emerge stronger from the US midterm elections, saying the vote mattered for the West as a whole.
Since taking office in 2023, Milei has laid off thousands of state employees , shut ministries, cut subsidies and reduced government-funded programmes. The measures were meant to fight high inflation, which has fallen to about 2 percent a month.
Milei says his plan is working, claiming that Argentina has grown for 27 consecutive months and is expanding at four times its historical rate.
When the coin crashed, Milei said he had acted “in good faith” and accused his political rivals of trying to exploit the situation.

The ⁠US defense department has designated Chinese-funded cultural centers on university campuses ⁠known as Confucius ⁠Institutes ​as a threat to US national security, defense secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth said on Friday.
Washington has long accused Confucius Institutes of being Chinese propaganda ⁠tools and has taken steps to ​crack down on them.
Hegseth, ‌in a ‌video posted on social media, alleged that Confucius ‌Institutes were operating under disguise at US universities and that the Pentagon had added them to its list of institutions that threaten US national security.
“It turns ‌out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped ​up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds ⁠of American students,” Hegseth said.
The defense department over ​the ​past two months has “systematically ​dismantled every single one of ​these organizations”, he ‌said.
The Chinese ​embassy ​in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: NASA Chief Warns China Is Closing Gap in ‘New Space Race’
articles.title_zh: NASA Chief Warns China Is Closing Gap in ‘New Space Race’
articles.content_orig:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman warned Friday that the United States is in a "new space race" with China, saying that the agency must recapture the urgency of the Apollo era if it hopes to return astronauts to the moon first.
China launched its first astronaut in 2003, he said, and has since built up a broad portfolio of space capabilities, including lunar missions and plans for a crewed moon landing before 2030. These rapid advances have created a competition far closer than the Cold War race that culminated in the Apollo moon landings, Isaacman said, during an Artemis update at Kennedy Space Center in Merritt Island, Florida.
"Nor will NASA sit idly by and watch one of the most consequential moments of this new century pass to our overseas competitors," he said. "The appetite for tolerating and defending the status quo has reached its conclusion."
NASA reaffirmed its summer plans for Artemis III, and for Artemis IV—the mission scheduled to return astronauts to the lunar surface—in 2028. The agency will continue to depend on Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to achieve these goals.
According to NASA officials, Artemis III will be a two-week mission involving four astronauts and a series of docking demonstrations in Earth's orbit, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing the lunar landers. The mission will not travel to the moon but is designed to test systems and operations needed for future lunar landings.
Artemis III will require multiple launches in quick succession from Florida and give crews an opportunity to conduct docking exercises with both commercial spacecraft, NASA leaders said.
During the briefing, Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons praised SpaceX's rapid development pace.
"We're seeing lots of hardware, lots of quick changes, and an absolute blistering pace of production," he said.
The agency's push comes as China works toward its publicly stated goal of landing astronauts on the moon before 2030, raising concerns among U.S. officials that America could lose momentum in a domain it once dominated.
Isaacman repeatedly invoked the Apollo era, arguing that NASA should draw lessons from when the agency progressed from Apollo 7's first crewed mission to Apollo 11's lunar landing within nine months.
"It's a playbook this agency knows really well, the same playbook that went from Apollo 7 splashdown to Apollo 11 in just nine months," he said.
While emphasizing that NASA will not compromise safety, Isaacman said the agency is working to cut bureaucracy, speed decision-making and increase the pace of hardware development.
The broader goal, he said, extends beyond simply returning astronauts to the moon.
"This will not be a repeat of flags and footprints," Isaacman said.
He described future lunar missions as laying the groundwork for a permanent human presence beyond Earth.
"These vehicles are being designed to dramatically reduce the cost of delivering mass to orbit and to the moon, to support longer surface operations, enable more frequent astronaut missions, and transform what will begin as a small scientific outpost into something that may one day resemble a city on the lunar surface, " Isaacman said.
Newsweek has reached out to the White House and SpaceX for comment.

articles.title_orig: Trump at South Florida rally revives the idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran
articles.title_zh: Trump at South Florida rally revives the idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran
articles.content_orig:
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s armed forces say they are prepared to fire on United States warships as President Donald Trump said Washington was still deliberating new attacks or continued pressure on Iran.
Trump told supporters at a rally in Florida on Friday that the US military “may do another Epic Fury”, in reference to the extensive bombing campaign against Iran at the start of the war. He had earlier questioned whether to end the conflict quickly through huge attacks on Iran or let pressure on Tehran from a naval blockade and sanctions persist.
But Ali Abdollahi, chief of general staff of the Iranian armed forces, asserted that the US Navy is incapable of re-entering Iran’s territorial waters or its periphery due to Iran’s ability to target any vessel in the region.
“The US president can only dream of their soldiers and military again entering the Persian Gulf. They will take this wish to the grave for good,” he said in a statement carried by state media on Saturday morning.
Abdollahi also said US rhetoric about the war pointed to a basic contradiction: US claims that Iran’s military capabilities have been mostly destroyed during the war were nullified by its refusal to bring its aircraft carriers and support vessels closer to Iranian territory.
He added that Iranian forces were determined to “drown” the US and Israel in a “quagmire” in retaliation for their surprise attack on Iran on February 28, starting an eight-month war and plunging the whole region into instability.
Vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue to be attacked by Iran. Together with the increased odds of renewed war, this has driven up oil prices and sent Brent crude to its highest price since April, at about $117.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said seven tankers were attacked or hit mines overnight into Thursday. It then claimed on Friday that two supertankers struck mines. The IRGC has said its military doctrine is now more offensive, and Washington has reportedly ordered many diplomatic personnel to leave Saudi Arabia, with others set to depart other countries in the region .
The Iran-allied Houthis in Yemen also continued to exchange attacks with Saudi Arabia, hitting Riyadh again on Saturday, with the international airport in Dammam and the Shaybah oilfield targeted in recent days. Saudi forces have bombed Marib, Taiz and several other Yemeni provinces under Houthi control.
In southern Lebanon, Friday brought further reported Israeli air attacks around Nabatieh and artillery fire near Zawtar ash-Sharqiyah. Iran has linked this front to its war with the US and Israel, in the past demanding that any ceasefire with Washington also cover Lebanon .
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, facing an election on October 27 which comes days before the November 3 mid-term elections in the US, also ordered a lockdown of the occupied West Bank after a Palestinian attack killed two soldiers in Hebron. The Houthis have also launched attacks on Israel linked to events in Gaza and the West Bank, highlighting how wider regional peace now depends on events in multiple theatres, including Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Netanyahu has reiterated his desire to overthrow the Iranian government, leading several state-linked media and analysts in Iran to claim that Tehran has activated a “dead hand” doctrine. That allegedly enables military attacks against US, Israeli and regional interests to continue from across the country’s 31 provinces if senior Iranian figures are again assassinated as at the start of the war .
The IRGC has threatened seabed internet and communication cables if Iran’s civilian infrastructure is again targeted by the US and Israel. US-based Axios on Saturday cited US intelligence claiming that Iranian authorities had “substantially increased” efforts to strike American officials in the Middle East and beyond.
Mediated negotiations between Iran and the US are no closer to yielding results. But regional and European powers held a coordination meeting in Istanbul on Friday and announced their expectations for the future of the war.
Top diplomats from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt met with the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy, with neither the US nor Iran participating.
“We agree that a new attack on Iran would widen the war and spread the conflict across the region,” Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said after the meeting. “Military intervention in Iran is by no means a solution. No one is endorsing it at this point.”
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said his government held Iran and the Houthis responsible for instability in the Middle East.
But the foreign ministers of the four regional countries issued a joint statement that said “Israeli occupation was the main source of instability in the region and beyond.”
In line with resolving the US-Israel war on Iran, the four regional countries supported the Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed in June and a negotiated settlement, while demanding unrestricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz . The group said they opposed attacks on civilians and commercial vessels, and condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and its Red Sea shipping interests.
The Istanbul meeting once again displayed a “gap between diplomatic claims and realities in the field”, Nour News, an outlet affiliated with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, argued in an analysis on Saturday.
It said the US and European powers – not Iran – must make concessions first. The outlet presented reopening the Strait of Hormuz as conditional on the US accepting Tehran’s demands and acknowledging responsibility for attacking Iran and Yemen.
Most Iranian newspapers on Saturday focused on signs of war, including rising oil prices.
The headline from hardline Vatan-e Emrooz reported that the price of a barrel of Brent crude rising above $117 was “evidence of disgrace for Trump”. Reformist Etemad said US and Israeli actions were signalling that the “zero hour” of another intense round of the war was approaching.
Reza Nasri, a Tehran-based foreign policy analyst with links to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that after being subject to decades of attacks, nuclear sabotage, sanctions and violated deals by the US, Iran’s strategy was now “enough is enough.
“Iran has reached its verdict. It will no longer negotiate under bombardment, honour agreements the other side treats as optional, or accept the killing of its children and the penury of its people as routine instruments of policy,” he wrote on X. “It will put an end to this cycle, and it will do so by all necessary means”.

articles.content_orig:
China’s remote access alone is expected to swell to 2.8 million H100-equivalents by the end of 2027, up from roughly 1 million this year
China’s access to artificial intelligence computing power will double next year, but US-designed chips will account for about 65 per cent of that capacity, an indication of its continued reliance on foreign hardware, according to new research.
Total compute available to Chinese entities was expected to expand in 2027 from about 4.6 million to 8.8 million “H100-equivalents” – a metric benchmarked against Nvidia’s data-centre graphics processing units, according to a report by the Washington-based Institute for Progress (IFP).
While the US maintains a roughly 16-fold advantage in AI training compute over China, leading Chinese models lag their American rivals by only 6.5 months, the report said.

articles.title_orig: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.title_zh: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.content_orig:
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.
A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.
Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.
All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.
More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said.
The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.
Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
In another development, Nigeria's health minister has said the country's single confirmed case of Ebola appears to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya.
Professor Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way.
He emphasised that Nigeria had so far recorded only one confirmed case of the virus.
"We are conducting additional tests. Some of the results are negative, while others are pending," Pate said.
Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria's first case crossed paths with Kenya's first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport earlier this month.

articles.title_zh: Patient dies in Bristol Myers Squibb autoimmune CAR-T trial
articles.content_orig:
Elaine’s stories explore the boom in new obesity treatments, new drug payment models, the ways companies are affected by FDA changes, and the emerging psychedelics drug sector. She co-writes The Readout newsletter , and co-hosts STAT’s weekly biotech podcast, The Readout Loud . You can reach Elaine on Signal at elaineywchen.70.
Bristol Myers Squibb on Friday reported that one patient died after receiving its investigational CAR-T therapy in an early autoimmune trial, adding to safety concerns about a growing field of research.
In a Phase 1 trial that tested the therapy in multiple sclerosis, a condition that causes muscle weakness and extreme fatigue, the patient experienced motor symptoms that did not resolve with standard autoimmune treatments. They were then given a potent immunosuppressant, but developed septic pneumonia and died, Bristol said in a press release.
In a subsequent statement sent to STAT, Bristol said this patient was treated for a series of other complications prior to receiving the CAR-T therapy, “confounding our ability to determine the root cause of the issue.”

articles.title_orig: Ruins of Limoges city hall a symbol of France divided by national protests
articles.title_zh: Ruins of Limoges city hall a symbol of France divided by national protests
articles.content_orig:
"It is a historical tragedy for France, not just Limoges".
Just six months into his mayoral term, it is hard to imagine Guillaume Guérin having a more momentous week.
We talk next to what became the defining image of last week's nationwide protests: the still impressive, yet fragile exterior of his town's 19th-Century town hall, charred from a fire.
The sight of its wooden clock tower collapsing into the flames drew widespread shock and anger, and Guérin, who was in tears when he first saw the scale of the damage this week, believes the reaction is "legitimate and completely understandable".
What is apparent from the array of flowers and sombre onlookers gathered at the hall's entrance, is that this is a town mourning the loss, or at the least the harm inflicted on its most iconic and, frankly, most beautiful building.
Guérin blames the damage on the French hard left, "supported by rioters". Two men have been arrested, a 66-year-old, as well as another suspect who is 34. Prosecutors say they have links to "radical-left networks".
Limoges' conservative mayor claims he has received a message of support from US Vice President JD Vance, but not Emmanual Macron, his own, outgoing president.
"What happened here will have an influence on the upcoming presidential election. This country is not doing well at all," he says.
For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become.
In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time.
In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening.
Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre.
Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone.
Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask.
"Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.
It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.
I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with €500,000 (£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?
"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.
Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."
She complains of having to live on €300 per month.
"I feel we are not respected as young adults."
Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.
This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.
In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stool here for more than a century.
"It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."
Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that.
"On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds.
Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease.
"Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork.
Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily.
Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement.
In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history will steer the demonstrations away from destruction and back to debate.
With France's political polarisation set to continue and further protests planned, it is a scenario far from assured.
Additional reporting by Paul Pradier.

US stocks declined on Friday as selling pressure broadened beyond the AI trade, while oil prices rose. The 10-year Treasury (^ TNX ) yield gained, though it held below the 5% threshold.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell more than 600 points, or 1.2%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) dropped 0.5%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) fell 0.2% after a steep decline in Tech (XLK) on Thursday.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted losses for a second week in a row, while the Dow ended the five-day stretch with gains.
The AI trade attempted a rebound following concerns over rising financing costs and a potential slowdown in capex, which weighed on already-battered neocloud stocks like CoreWeave ( CRWV ). Shares of AI chip giants Nvidia ( NVDA ) and AMD ( AMD ) closed the session mixed after Thursday's sell-off.
Shares of this week's earnings headliners, SpaceX ( SPCX ), Tesla ( TSLA ), and Meta ( META ), stabilized in Friday trading after declining in the previous session.
Not all of tech was struggling, though. Cybersecurity stocks, including SailPoint ( SAIL ), Cloudflare ( NET ), and Palo Alto Networks ( PANW ), each rose more than 7%.
Oil prices remained near a five-month high amid fears of escalating tensions in the Middle East, with Brent crude ( BZ=F ) futures for December delivery closing just north of $116 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) climbed above $103 per barrel.
The prospect of higher energy costs weighed on transportation stocks, with shares of United ( UAL ), Delta ( DAL ), and American ( AAL ) all falling.
The major averages fell on Friday as higher oil prices weighed on sentiment ahead of next week's Fed policy meeting.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 1.2%, while those for the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) dropped 0.5%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) decreased 0.2% following a steep sell-off in semiconductors and other tech stocks on Thursday.
Brent crude ( BZ=F ) futures for December delivery settled at a six-month high of $116.72 per barrel. Meanwhile, West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) closed just above $103 a barrel.
Treasury yields moved higher, although the 10-year yield remained below 5%.
Investors will turn their attention to the Federal Reserve's policy meeting next week, with markets widely expecting the central bank to leave interest rates unchanged.
Oil prices climbed to a six-month high on Friday as traders priced the odds of escalating fighting in the Middle East. Attacks near the Red Sea also stoked worries of further constraints on oil supplies from the region.
Brent crude ( BZ=F ) futures for December delivery settled at $116.72 per barrel. The international benchmark posted its third consecutive week of gains. Meanwhile, West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) closed just above $103 a barrel.
Cybersecurity stocks jumped on Friday, with SailPoint ( SAIL ), Cloudflare ( NET ), and Palo Alto Networks ( PANW ) each rising more than 7%.
The move came alongside an Evercore ISI survey that found a strengthening budget outlook for security. According to the survey, spending is aimed at securing data, AI, identities, and cloud.
Okta ( OKTA ) and Fortinet ( FTNT ) were two of the channel partners with strong pipelines.
Cybersecurity stocks have been on fire this year, fueled by AI-driven spending and growing warnings from tech giants about the risks of increasingly powerful agents.
The First Trust Cybersecurity ETF ( CIBR ) reached an all-time high earlier this month. Over the past five days, the CIBR is up roughly 7%.
Yahoo Finance's Ben Werschkul reports:
President Trump, for the second day in a row, telegraphed an escalation in Iran after the midterm elections and an extended standoff, with the Strait of Hormuz still at the center of the conflict.
"The question is: Do we want to finish it off or do we just want to let it wither because we're getting everything we wanted," the president told reporters on Friday morning as he touted evidence of Middle East oil exports surpassing prewar levels.
The comments also came after Trump's ambassador to the UN told the Financial Times that the war could last another year and that the US is prepared for a long-term standoff, but that he hoped negotiations would end the conflict sooner.
Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian reports:
SpaceX ( SPCX ) investors have had a rocky week. A third-quarter report that beat estimates and Elon Musk's open backing of a merger with Tesla ( TSLA ) sent shares surging Wednesday, but a Thursday sell-off erased the gain.
Shares climbed slightly on Friday amid news that the company's mobile aspirations are picking up. Bloomberg reports the company is looking to lease space on 80,000 cell sites across the US to build out a terrestrial network. SpaceX is reportedly in talks with two of the largest owners of cellular towers, Crown Castle and American Tower.
In its Q3 report, SpaceX reported that Connectivity revenue, mostly from Starlink, rose 69% to $5.2 billion. President Gwynne Shotwell said Starlink added 1.6 million subscribers in the quarter, bringing the total to just under 14 million broadband consumer subscribers.
Moderna ( MRNA ) trimmed losses Friday, rebounding from a sharp sell-off in the previous session, as investors digested data from a late-stage trial of its personalized melanoma vaccine.
The stock opened lower but climbed into positive territory during the session, a day after plunging more than 17% on Thursday in its worst single-day performance since Aug. 20.
Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre reports:
In July, SK Hynix ( SKHY ) raised $26.5 billion in the biggest US listing ever by a foreign company. Now the company is walking away from one of the biggest tech IPOs ever.
The South Korean memory giant said Friday it has shelved plans to list Solidigm, its flash memory unit, in the US, citing market conditions and share price trends. Solidigm had aimed to raise $10 billion to $15 billion at a valuation of up to $150 billion, according to industry estimates cited by the Wall Street Journal .
For a clue to why, look at the company's own stock.
SK Hynix priced its US shares at $149 in July. SK Hynix stock is rising on Friday but still trades below that price, about a third below the stock's September record.
Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre reports:
Apple ( AAPL ) is taking Wall Street's crown back from Nvidia — for the fifth time.
Apple briefly topped Nvidia in market value on Friday. It's a move Apple has made before, and it has rarely stuck.
Apple and Nvidia ( NVDA ) are each worth about $5.1 trillion, and the gap between them was less than 1% at Thursday's close. The flip came alongside a record run for Apple's stock and the day the tech giant's $1,999 iPhone Duo hit stores , capping a battle investors had been watching all morning. Nvidia has since moved back into the lead.
Shares of American Express ( AXP ) fell 3% Friday after the credit card giant delivered third quarter results and said it plans to eliminate roughly 5% of its workforce globally as part of a restructuring effort.
American Express CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts the cuts are part of a restructuring effort to make the company a "more agile and efficient organization." As part of the effort, the firm recognized a $336 million restructuring charge in the third quarter.
A company spokesperson told Yahoo Finance the reduction will eliminate 3,500 roles globally.
Squeri added that earlier this year he asked senior executives to find ways to cut corporate bloat across the company in order to refocus on American Express' biggest priorities.
Earlier this month, federal bank regulators fined the credit card giant $350 million over widespread failures in its anti-money laundering controls.
In the third quarter, American Express reported revenue climbed 9% to $14.5 billion from a year ago while adjusted earnings per share rose 13% to $4.68. Analysts were expecting $14.8 billion in revenue.

Abbas Araqchi, Foreign Minister of the Islamic Republic, stated on Wednesday, October 21, that “the country is truly in a state of war,” adding that hostilities remain ongoing as Iran simultaneously confronts military threats and extensive economic sanctions.
In remarks reported by domestic Iranian media outlets, Araqchi said: “Under current conditions, the country is facing both war and military threats alongside widespread economic sanctions. At present, the reality is that the country is truly in a state of war, and the war is still ongoing.”
In response to a question regarding Tehran’s latest reply to the United States concerning negotiations, the Foreign Minister stated that the Islamic Republic has delivered its proposal to Washington, and the onus now lies on the U.S. to meet Tehran’s conditions.
“Our response is clear,” Araqchi noted. “We have submitted our proposal to the United States. If they are sincere about advancing negotiations and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, they must fulfill our conditions for everything to be resolved.”
Reiterating Tehran’s position against American pressure, Araqchi added: “Everyone knows that we will not surrender.”

articles.title_orig: Irish politicians disavow ‘demeaning’ PSA warning grandparents not to hug family without asking consent
articles.title_zh: Irish politicians disavow ‘demeaning’ PSA warning grandparents not to hug family without asking consent
articles.content_orig:
Multiple politicians from the Irish government have disavowed an ad from a state-funded organization warning against hugging one's family members without consent.
An ad released by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) in Ireland that urged grandparents to ask for consent before hugging their grandchildren sparked international controversy after it began airing last month and has since been removed.
In September, an ad from the DRCC’s We-Consent campaign went viral for showing grandparents greeting their grandchildren. One grandchild appears receptive to a hug, while the other does not. A narrator says, "Not everyone wants a hug, even from the people who love them. Awkward? Maybe. Important? Absolutely."
The ad has since been removed and criticized by politicians from multiple parties in Ireland.
The BBC reported that Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan of the Fianna Fáil party, whose department funded the campaign, announced the video has been removed after discussion with the DRCC, and declared, it "does not represent the views of the Government."
IRISH PM SAYS IRELAND 'NOT OVERRUN' BY MIGRANTS, LEGAL MIGRATION TIED TO ECONOMIC SUCCESS
The ad showed grandparents greeting their grandchildren, one of whom appeared happy to receive affection. (Screenshot/Dublin Rape Crisis Centre ad)
"It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my officials engagement with them," O'Callaghan said. "While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive."
Irish Sen. Gareth Scahill of the Fine Gael party blasted the video as a waste of public funds.
"What's concerning here is public money has been used to fund an ad which, at best, has been ill-thought out, and at worst is offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," Scahill said.
"The issue of consent is a very serious one, and I acknowledge the important work the Rape Crisis Centre and other agencies do every day to advocate for all victims of rape and sexual violence, including children.
"But this publicly funded social media video is a million miles off the mark."
TRUMP SAYS HE WOULD 'LOVE' TO SEE IRELAND UNIFIED AS ONE NATION
The other grandchild who appeared in the commercial did not appear to want a hug from her grandparents. (Screenshot/Dublin Rape Crisis Centre ad)
Scahill also asked, "What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls in Dublin, Shannon, Knock and Cork airports this Christmas before we can greet family members?"
The DRCC told Irish broadcaster RTE in a statement, "We-Consent is a long-term campaign as part of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's prevention work to increase the awareness and practice of consent in Ireland.
"We created three videos premised on the idea that boundaries should be respected from an early age and to respect others' boundaries too," the organization added. "We are going to remove the videos from our social media channels while we reflect on whether they are having the positive effect we want them to have."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE
The ad has been widely panned online and disavowed by Irish politicians from multiple parties. (Screenshot/Dublin Rape Crisis Centre ad)
Inez Stepman, senior policy and legal analyst at Independent Women, spoke with Fox News Digital about the controversy.
"Instead of honestly acknowledging what is behind the doubling of rape rates from a decade ago, which is who the government chooses to let into the country, these institutions lecture grandparents about hugging their grandkids, as though that has any remotest connection to the problem at hand," she said.
In 2024, The Irish Independent reported that reports of sexual assault had nearly doubled in Ireland between 2012 and 2022.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
"This politically correct lack of courage and honesty is embarrassing and rightly caused a backlash," Stepman added.
Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

articles.title_orig: Alleged Chinese agent Wanying Zhang pleads not guilty in Los Angeles courtroom
articles.title_zh: Alleged Chinese agent Wanying Zhang pleads not guilty in Los Angeles courtroom
articles.content_orig:
A Southern California realtor accused of being a Chinese foreign agent pleaded not guilty to the allegations in a Los Angeles federal courtroom Friday.
Wanying Zhang, 34, appeared in a white jumpsuit and shackles, speaking only to deny charges that she surveilled the Taiwanese president's son in a Seattle suburb in September 2025.
The plea puts the case on track for a trial that will require the Justice Department to lay out its evidence of the allegations she conspired with Chinese intelligence officials for what prosecutors called a spy mission.
She was arrested earlier this month at L.A. International Airport while attempting to board a flight to China. She has been charged with one count of acting in the U.S. as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government.
Zhang's husband, Edric Ding, had appeared in earlier court hearings. The couple have been realtors together at the same firm in Irvine, California.
But Ding did not appear at the short hearing on Friday. This is after prosecutors claimed in a recent court filing that Zhang was having an affair with a man who accompanied her on the alleged surveillance mission to Washington state last year. CBS has identified him as Fatai Miao, a construction entrepreneur who recently left Southern California on a one-way ticket to China.
Miao's son told CBS News he does not believe his father was working for the Chinese government, and Miao has not been charged with any crime.
The judge set a pretrial hearing for Nov. 12. The trial is scheduled to begin Nov. 30 at a federal courthouse in Santa Ana, California, and will last an estimated four days.
Both prosecutors and Zhang's attorney, Craig Harbaugh, declined to comment on Friday.

articles.title_orig: Time ‘running out’ to reach Yemen’s Taiz amid deepening crisis, UN says
articles.title_zh: Time ‘running out’ to reach Yemen’s Taiz amid deepening crisis, UN says
articles.content_orig:
Taiz, Yemen – It was approaching 10:30am in the dialysis centre of the Republican Hospital in Taiz when a machine began filtering excess fluids, toxins and salts from the blood of Omar Mukhtar Hammoud.
The 16-year-old suffers from kidney failure and is one of 270 patients who regularly receive dialysis at the centre in the government-held city in southwest Yemen. But with essential medical supplies and fuel running critically low under the renewed Houthi siege , doctors fear they may soon be unable to provide the treatment that keeps their patients alive.
Dr Essam Mahyoub Dahan, the centre’s director, warned that a complete shutdown could happen within days.
“Because of the siege and the shortage of diesel and medical solutions, we have recently been forced to reduce dialysis sessions from four hours to just two and a half,” Dahan told Al Jazeera. “We know this is not adequate, but we have no choice if we are to keep the centre operating for as long as possible before it shuts down completely.”
Dahan said the centre’s remaining stocks of specialised dialysis solutions were also close to running out.
The supplies, which are expensive, are normally provided by the Yemeni Ministry of Health every three months. But the latest delivery which was due earlier this month  failed to arrive because of the Houthi siege on Taiz city. It began in the first week of October after Houthi advances in the Taiz countryside.
The city was previously under complete Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, in the early years of Yemen’s ongoing war.
Across Taiz governorate, where battles are raging between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iranian-allied Houthi fighters, the number of patients at risk is far greater.
In an October 12 statement, the governorate’s health office warned that the continued siege and obstruction of essential supplies could endanger the lives of 1,110 patients with kidney failure. They depend on dialysis services in the governorate’s hospitals, which collectively provide about 210 dialysis sessions a day.
International humanitarian and health organisations have issued similar warnings about the impact of the siege on the already fragile healthcare system in Taiz.
On Thursday, Amnesty International called on the Houthis to immediately reopen vital roads into and around the city, warning that the closure of the main road between Taiz and the southern port city of Aden threatened hundreds of thousands of civilians with losing access to food, water and healthcare.
Taiz’s hospitals depend heavily on diesel-powered generators because much of the city’s electricity infrastructure was destroyed during the war that began 11 years ago and has not been restored.
The renewed Houthi siege has severely disrupted the entry of fuel, including the diesel needed to run hospital generators and lifesaving medical equipment.
Dr Shaheed al-Ameri, deputy director-general for technical affairs at the Republican Hospital, said the shortages have had a devastating impact on medical services.
“A very large part of this suffering is because of the shortage of diesel,” he told Al Jazeera. “We have no reserve diesel supplies. Our stocks ran out early in the siege and we are now buying it on the black market almost every day, at prices that have reached five times what they were before the siege.”
Al-Ameri warned that the longer the siege continues, the more prices will rise and the further medical services will deteriorate.
The hospital has already suspended operations in some departments, including essential units, he said.
“If this situation continues much longer, we fear we will reach a complete and comprehensive collapse of healthcare services,” he said.
The shortages are not confined to the Republican Hospital. On October 22, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies were threatening lifesaving healthcare throughout  Taiz governorate, with some hospital services already disrupted.
According to the WHO, 42 health facilities in Taiz city had reported severe shortages of essential supplies. Hospitals and ambulances require at least 156,000 litres of fuel a month to continue functioning.
The organisation also warned that diesel shortages threaten to disrupt oxygen production, water pumping, vaccine refrigeration and sanitation services, increasing the risks of disease outbreaks, particularly among displaced families and other vulnerable groups.
The United Nations has separately warned that the restrictions on supplies are bringing Taiz’s health system close to collapse and urged the Houthis to allow humanitarian assistance and essential goods to enter without obstruction.
In its October 12 statement, Taiz’s health office warned that continued restrictions on fuel deliveries could lead to the shutdown of medical oxygen production plants, further endangering patients.
Taysir al-Samei, the health office’s media officer, said that would dramatically worsen the crisis.
“Many medical departments depend on oxygen, particularly operating theatres, inpatient wards, intensive care units and incubators for premature babies,” al-Samei said.
“Most hospitals have already suspended services in some units because of the shortage of diesel and the lack of necessary medical solutions, as well as shortages of medical staff who are struggling to get to work because of the lack of transport,” he added.
He warned that if conditions continued to deteriorate at the same pace, some hospitals could stop providing services in the coming days.
At the Republican Hospital, al-Ameri said that shortages were also affecting diagnostics and treatment. The availability of laboratory reagents had fallen to just 10 to 15 percent of previous levels, he said, while approximately half of the medicines normally available were now out of stock.
Prices for the remaining medicines had doubled, he said, placing them further out of reach for patients already struggling with Yemen’s worsening economic crisis.
The continued fighting and shelling around Taiz have increased the number of wounded people requiring emergency care – placing additional pressure on facilities already struggling with shortages of surgical supplies , anaesthetics and intravenous fluids.
Abdul Badi Abdulwuhab, 53, is another dialysis patient in the Republican Hospital, struggling to cope with the shorter dialysis sessions.
His voice was filled with desperation.
“Because of these measures, I suffer from weakness and I cannot bear the pain,” Abdul Badi told Al Jazeera. “Two and a half hours is not enough to remove all the fluids and toxins from my body.”
Dr Dahan said that the patient’s condition had deteriorated since his sessions were shortened.
“These measures are not effective for many patients,” Dahan said. “The only solution is to end the siege and return things to the way they were.”

articles.title_orig: US discreetly moves diplomats and families from multiple Middle Eastern countries as escalation fears grow
articles.title_zh: US discreetly moves diplomats and families from multiple Middle Eastern countries as escalation fears grow
articles.content_orig:
The United States is rushing to move some diplomats and their family members from posts in the Middle East as the threat of regional escalation looms, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.
The departures have been described as a frustrating and chaotic déjà vu, as many of those leaving had only recently returned to their posts after being ordered out during the height of the Iran war.
An unclassified October 23 memo to Secretary of State Marco Rubio says US intelligence has found that “Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel” and plotting efforts “have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries.”
A US official told CNN, “When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment. The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region.”
Axios was first to report on the unclassified memo.
“To say it has been chaotic is an understatement,” said one US diplomat, explaining that the financial support they have been offered to date does not cover the costs for moving their entire family from the region. Many of those families had scrambled then to leave their homes in the Middle East in the early weeks of the war and find new housing and schools for their kids. Now, many are having to do the same again, with what they say is potentially less financial support from the State Department.
“This echoes the chaos families experienced earlier this year. Some had barely settled back in before being told to leave again,” Nikki Gamer, the spokesperson for the American Foreign Service Association, told CNN. “They are understandably upset, confused, and angry.”
Later Friday, a State Department official confirmed that all US direct hire personnel and their families “are getting per diem allowances and support for lodging and schools, with per diem allowances consistent with government rates of where they are geographically in the country.”
The adjustments come as the Iranian-backed Houthis have increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia – hostilities which the State Department has repeatedly warned “have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”
They also come as US President Donald Trump has suggested he could relaunch strikes against Iran after the midterms, and as sources said Israel has lobbied – unsuccessfully for now – for more immediate action.
The State Department this week ordered the departure of non-emergency personnel and all family members from Saudi Arabia. Officials said the ordered departure was done in response to the Houthi escalations.
At the same time, it has been quietly adjusting its staffing caps at multiple other embassies in the Middle East, including Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, and Lebanon, sources told CNN.
A State Department official confirmed to CNN that Lebanon, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Jordan “will see temporary changes to staffing levels under restricted operations.” They said there are no changes to personnel in Kuwait or Bahrain, which suggest they are not over their staffing caps.
“Under Restricted Operations Status, staffing levels are constantly evaluated and adjusted,” the official said.
Unlike the Saudi Arabia ordered departure, the movements from these embassies have not been publicly announced. The State Department has stressed that those embassies, unlike Saudi Arabia, have not changed status and remain on “restricted operations” status. Even when there is no formal change in status, there can still be a change in staffing within the “restricted operations” status.
“There’s a very Groundhog Day vibe,” a source in Amman said of some embassy staff being asked to leave the Jordanian capital again.
Not all of the embassies allowed children to return to the posts, but most allowed spouses to come back. Now, the family members are leaving those embassies to which they have only recently been allowed to return – but unlike earlier this year, sources say family members are not being given the same financial support.
Communication and coordination around the departures from the department’s headquarters in Foggy Bottom to foreign service officers in the field is “just as much of a shit show” as early on in the Iran war, said one source familiar with the departures.
In the days around the adjustments, there were concerns among foreign service officers about whether the State Department will give their families “per diem” allowances for relocating to the US, the source said, noting that some embassies haven’t had the planning meetings or town halls with staff that are typical before departures.
“A lot of people are hearing about it through the news instead of their leadership at post,” the source added.
The American Foreign Service Association, the union representing foreign service officers, said it is hearing accounts “of bureaucratic ping-pong.”
“Families that had barely returned to their posts and re-enrolled their children in school are being told to prepare to evacuate again without being advised as to what level of financial support they can count on,” it said in a statement Thursday.
Gamer, the spokesperson for AFSA, told CNN that “families outside Saudi Arabia have told AFSA they are being directed to leave without confirmed housing assistance or per diem.” They have been told this is because their embassies are not changing status from “restricted operations.”
Families often rely on those allowances to help them find housing and cover the unexpected costs associated with being uprooted from their homes abroad, especially if their diplomatic family member is remaining at the embassy as an essential worker.
“Families deserve to know how they will pay for a place to live before they board a plane,” Gamer said.
The State Department official said, “We understand how hard being on Restricted Operations Status, Authorized Departure, or Ordered Departure is for our diplomatic staff and their families.”
“We are committed to using every tool available to help families navigate this difficult time, including the added expenses and school enrollment,” they said. “We are communicating directly with staff affected by these latest changes and will have more to say in the days ahead.”
This story has been updated with additional details.
